video_title: Horizon Robotics CEO: Car Chips, Mind-Off Driving and China's Speed | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Horizon Robotics CEO Yukai explains why neutral, safety-qualified auto compute is a high-barrier business with Chinese share near one in three cars, lays out hands-off (2028), eyes-off (2030) and mind-off (2035) targets, and argues the auto supply chain will carry China into robotics.

themes.theme: Auto chip moat and cycle economics

insights.claim: Horizon Robotics says its chips run roughly one in three cars in China, with customers including BYD, Great Wall and other Chinese OEMs plus global OEMs Volkswagen, Toyota and Suzuki.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Gives a market-share anchor for the leading independent Chinese ADAS silicon vendor.

insights.claim: Horizon Robotics' CEO says China's automotive computing market has consolidated to three main players: Nvidia, Huawei and Horizon Robotics.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Domestic ADAS compute is an oligopoly, limiting new-entrant pricing pressure.
insights.quote: really consolidated to uh Nvidia, Huawei and Horizon Robotics

insights.claim: Automotive chip development takes 3-4 years to get the chip and solution ready, then 3-5 years of production cycle for the car platform (about 2 years in China, around 5 for global OEMs), so the total cycle from start to revenue is at least five years and up to eight.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Long design-in cycles mean backlog is visible years out and share shifts slowly once locked in.
insights.quote: So then think about it's going to be at least from five years to 80 years for the cycle

insights.claim: Horizon's CEO argues that slow, capital-heavy, safety-qualified automotive silicon is 'a terrible business that is a great business' because the high entry barrier keeps VC-funded newcomers out.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Moat comes from qualification and safety standards, not technology alone; supports pricing durability.
insights.quote: terrible business means a great business

insights.claim: Horizon positions itself as a fabless platform supplier (designing chips plus end-to-end neural-network driving software, outsourcing manufacturing) with about 2,000 employees, mostly engineers, and deliberately does not build cars, modelling itself on Windows/Intel for PCs and Arm/Android for mobile.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: A neutral supplier to all OEMs can scale across brands, unlike vertically integrated Xpeng or Xiaomi.
insights.quote: I always position ourself going to be like a Microsoft and Intel

insights.claim: Horizon's stated roadmap is hands-off driving by end of 2028, eyes-off by end of 2030 and fully mind-off (sleeping in the car) by end of 2035, framed for consumers rather than SAE levels.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Gives dated milestones against which Chinese ADAS adoption and compute demand can be tracked.

insights.claim: Horizon's latest stack, Horizon SuperDrive on the Journey 6T SoC, already delivers a completely hands-free experience, and the CEO expects essentially all passenger vehicles in China to be hands-free within two years.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies rapid mass-market penetration of advanced ADAS in China and rising compute content per car.
insights.quote: by the end of uh the all the passenger vehicles in China will be hands-free

insights.claim: The CEO says the bottleneck to eyes-off driving is not core capability but accumulating far larger test mileage and statistics to prove safety.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Regulatory and validation data, not algorithms, gate the next autonomy step.
insights.quote: we need a much bigger you know mileage to test and prove uh eyes off

insights.claim: Progress in autonomous driving needs three factors together: much more on-vehicle compute, continuously growing high-quality data focused on corner cases, and larger models by parameter count.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports rising in-car compute and data-loop investment as structural demand drivers.

themes.theme: China competitive intensity and supply chain

insights.claim: China's car market has roughly 60-70 brands and more than 580 new car models launched in the first half of 2026, driven by competition plus consumer demand for smart features like automated parking and autonomous driving.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Extreme OEM competition pushes smart-driving features down-market, favoring the shared chip supplier over individual brands.
insights.quote: more than 580 new car models launched

insights.claim: Horizon's CEO says Chinese OEMs cut model cycles to about two years versus roughly five for European OEMs, attributing it to intense competition, hard work and no long summer vacations.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Speed gap is a core competitive threat to Western automakers.

insights.claim: China's automotive supply chain is so deep that a new idea can always find component or technology partners quickly, and the CEO treats the whole country as one village given three-hour flights between Beijing and Shenzhen.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Supply-chain density, not only labor cost, underpins Chinese hardware iteration speed.
insights.quote: China nowadays is like a wonderland for supply chain

insights.claim: In China any business that looks even somewhat interesting attracts hundreds of competitors, as seen in embodied AI and humanoid robots, which is why Horizon deliberately picks areas with high entry barriers.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Crowded Chinese humanoid and EV markets imply margin compression and shakeouts for most entrants.

insights.claim: Horizon says it does not compete with European semiconductor firms Infineon, NXP and STMicro, who focus on analog and MCUs, and urges a 'win-win' mindset in which Western and Chinese firms jointly explore new markets rather than extract profit from each other.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals Horizon seeks partnerships with Europeans, e.g. Volkswagen, as a route to ex-China growth.

insights.claim: Horizon claims to be one of the top two players in China in generic robotics computing, supplying chips (not software) to robot makers, while its current business is nearly 100% passenger vehicles.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Robotics is optionality, not yet material revenue.

insights.claim: The CEO argues that cars and humanoid robots will converge onto a unifying computing platform, and that winning the automotive supply chain (actuators, sensors, lidar, radar) means winning robotics, as mobile-phone supply chain winners later won in IoT.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Auto-scale cost curves in components could give Chinese suppliers a robotics cost edge.
insights.quote: going to be winner for for for robotics

insights.claim: Horizon's CEO estimates meaningful volumes of humanoid robots are about five years away if optimistic, and says he is more conservative than peers; home service and elderly care in a rapidly ageing China are the top use cases.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: A conservative timeline from a chip supplier tempers humanoid hype and suggests slow near-term chip volumes.
insights.quote: five years if uh if uh optimistic

insights.claim: The CEO rejects a zero-sum US-China robotics framing, arguing US robotics firms that work with China's manufacturing ecosystem would innovate faster than those relying on slower supply chains.
insights.speaker: Yukai (Horizon Robotics CEO)
insights.so_what: Reflects a Chinese supplier's view on decoupling risk; not evidence of policy outcome.
